ECE 6390

Reading coding gain at a fixed error rate

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows the bit-error curves of uncoded BPSK and of a rate-1/2 code with minimum distance 10, and the horizontal gap between them at a target error rate of 10⁻⁶.

A coding-performance plot shows post-decoder bit-error rate against energy per information bit. Choose the target error rate the application needs, read the Eb,info/N₀ each design requires at that rate, and subtract: G_c = (Eb/N₀)_uncoded − (Eb,info/N₀)_coded, in decibels. The gain is the transmit power the code saves, or the extra margin it buys, at that reliability.

Both curves must use energy per information bit. A rate-r code sends 1/r coded bits per information bit, so at fixed power and information rate each coded bit carries Eb,coded = r·Eb,info. Plotting the coded curve against Eb,coded/N₀ shifts it by 10·log₁₀(1/r), 3.01 dB for r = 1/2, and would claim a gain the code does not deliver.

For soft-decision maximum-likelihood decoding of BPSK in white Gaussian noise, the leading union-bound term is P_b ≈ B·Q(√(2r·d·Eb,info/N₀)), where d is the minimum distance and B counts information-bit errors among the nearest error events. As the target tightens, the gain approaches the asymptotic value 10·log₁₀(r·d). The multiplicity B keeps the practical gain below that value at moderate error rates.

A code’s family name alone does not fix its gain. Block or memory length, distance, decoder quality and complexity all matter, and a capacity bound gives only a ceiling. A link budget should spend only the gain read from a curve for the actual code, decoder and target.

Example

Uncoded BPSK needs 10.53 dB for a 10⁻⁶ bit-error rate. A rate-1/2 code with d = 10 and B = 36, close to the common constraint-length-7 convolutional code, needs about 4.7 dB, a coding gain of about 5.8 dB. Its asymptotic gain is 10·log₁₀(5) = 6.99 dB.

Practice

1. A rate-3/4 code has minimum distance 5. What is its asymptotic soft-decision coding gain?

Use 10·log₁₀(r·d).

10·log₁₀(0.75 × 5) = 10·log₁₀(3.75) ≈ 5.74 dB. The gain at a practical error rate will be somewhat smaller.

2. Why must a coded curve be plotted against Eb,info/N₀ rather than Eb,coded/N₀ when computing coding gain?

Count the coded bits sent per information bit at fixed received power.

The comparison concerns the energy spent per useful bit. Each coded bit of a rate-r code carries only r times the information-bit energy, so the coded-bit axis credits the code with 10·log₁₀(1/r) dB it does not save.
